title: Chapter 4: The Intractable 2
content:
Chapter 4

The Intractable 2

Wei Wuxian’s first thought was that the kids had botched their flag formation.

His inventions were volatile beasts; a single misplaced stroke or minor mishandling could invite catastrophe. That was the whole reason he had double-checked the talisman strokes earlier. So, when rough hands seized his collar and dragged him across the flagstones, Wei Wuxian went entirely limp, letting them haul him like a sack of grain—at least it spared him the walking.

They dumped him into the Eastern Hall, which was absolute bedlam. The crowd rivaled the village mob from that afternoon. Servants and clan relations were crammed wall to wall, some still in their night robes with their hair undone, their faces gray with panic. Madam Mo was slumped across her seat as though she’d just surfaced from a dead faint. Tear tracks still streaked her powdered cheeks, but the second Wei Wuxian was hauled over the threshold, that grief sharpened into pure venom.

In the center of the room lay a human shape draped beneath a white sheet, only the head exposed. Lan Sizhui and his fellow disciples were leaning over it, their expressions grim, murmuring in urgent undertones.

Fragments drifted into Wei Wuxian’s ears:

“…Found less than half an incense stick ago?”

“We’d just subdued the walking corpses in the Western Courtyard. As we rushed east, we tripped over him right in the corridor.”

The body was Mo Ziyuan. Wei Wuxian took one look, then found himself looking again.

It looked like Mo Ziyuan, yet it didn’t. The facial structure clearly belonged to his obnoxious cousin, but the cheeks were sunken hollow, the eyes bulged from their sockets, and the skin was shriveled and leathery. Compared to the swaggering brat from yesterday, this corpse looked twenty years older. It was as though every drop of blood and vitality had been sucked bone-dry, leaving a gaunt skeleton wrapped in parchment skin. If Mo Ziyuan had merely been unsightly in life, in death he was both hideous and ancient.

As Wei Wuxian leaned in to scrutinize the details, a flash of steel caught his eye. Madam Mo lunged at him, a dagger brandished in her grip. Lan Sizhui moved like lightning, swatting the blade from her hand before she could strike.

Before the disciple could even speak, Madam Mo shrieked into his face, “My son was murdered! I am going to avenge him! Why are you protecting him?!”

Wei Wuxian dropped into a quick squat behind Lan Sizhui's robes. “Your son died a grisly death—what does that have to do with me?”

Lan Sizhui had witnessed Wei Wuxian’s manic breakdown that afternoon and had since heard all the colorful, exaggerated village gossip about the bastard nephew. He felt a deep surge of pity for the poor lunatic, prompting him to step in. “Madam Mo, look at your son’s corpse. His flesh, blood, and essence have been drained dry—he was clearly slaughtered by a malevolent entity. This could not have been his doing.”

Madam Mo’s chest heaved. “What do you little brats know?! That madman’s father was a cultivator, and he’s learned plenty of crooked sorcery of his own!”

Lan Sizhui glanced back at Wei Wuxian, who was playing the part of a slack-jawed idiot, and reasoned gently, “Madam, you have no proof. Perhaps we should—”

“The proof is right on my son’s body!” Madam Mo pointed a trembling finger at the sheet. “Look for yourselves! A-Yuan’s corpse tells me exactly who murdered him!”

Without waiting for permission, Wei Wuxian reached out and yanked the sheet back from head to toe.

Mo Ziyuan was missing a piece.

His entire left arm was gone—severed clean from the shoulder down!

Madam Mo cried, “Do you see it now?! You were all standing right here today—you heard him! What did this psycho say? He swore that if A-Yuan ever touched his things again, he’d chop his arm off!”

Her fury gave way to choking sobs. She covered her face, weeping, “…My poor, innocent A-Yuan never touched a single thing belonging to that freak! He was framed, and then that lunatic slaughtered him in cold blood…”

In cold blood!

It had been an eternity since someone had thrown that label in his face; hearing it now felt weirdly nostalgic. Wei Wuxian pointed at his own nose, thoroughly speechless. He honestly couldn't tell whether he was the crazy one or Madam Mo was. When he was younger, he’d barked plenty of dramatic threats about wiping out entire bloodlines, leaving mountains of corpses, and filling rivers with blood—but ninety percent of it was pure posturing. If talking the talk meant walking the walk, he would have ruled the entire cultivation world decades ago. Madam Mo wasn't looking for justice; she was just hunting for a convenient scapegoat to take her rage out on.

Refusing to waste breath arguing, Wei Wuxian crouched down, reached straight into Mo Ziyuan’s breast robe, and fished around. His fingers snagged on cloth. He drew it out and shook it flat.

A Spirit Attraction Flag.

Everything clicked. Wei Wuxian shook his head in silent contempt: You reap what you sow, idiot.

The Lan disciples took one look at the flag and the puzzle pieces fell into place. Connecting the dots from today’s circus wasn't hard: Mo Ziyuan had lost face after the public confrontation, simmering with humiliation and plotting payback. But Mo Xuanyu had wandered off to loaf around the village, vanishing until dusk. Mo Ziyuan must have planned to ambush him in the dead of night to settle the score.

Creeping out after dark, he would have slipped past the Western Courtyard and spotted the black banners fluttering on the eaves. Even though he’d been warned multiple times not to leave his room, not to approach the courtyard, and under no circumstances to touch the flags, Mo Ziyuan had assumed the cultivators were merely gatekeeping some priceless treasure. Ignorant of the flag's grim nature, he had no clue that stuffing one into his collar essentially turned him into a walking beacon for death. Greedy by habit, and addicted to looting talismans from his cousin, he couldn't resist. While the cultivators were occupied with rounding up the corpses inside the yard, he’d quietly snatched one off the wall.

The disciples had set up an array of six banners: five placed throughout the courtyard using themselves as bait, shielded by a web of high-grade spiritual talismans and clan relics. Mo Ziyuan, armed with nothing but his own arrogance, had swaggered off with the sixth. Evil spirits naturally go after the easiest prey. Had it been a standard walking corpse, a bite or two wouldn't have killed him instantly; he could have been saved. But luck was not on his side. The stolen banner had lured in something far darker and infinitely more vicious than a shambling corpse—an unknown monstrosity that drained him dry and ripped away his left arm.

Wei Wuxian casually tugged back his left sleeve. Sure enough, the slash marks crisscrossing his wrist had vanished, the flesh smooth and whole. The blood pact of the sacrificial ritual had officially credited Mo Ziyuan’s death to him. Since the Spirit Attraction Flag was his original design anyway, it technically counted as a kill by proxy.

Madam Mo knew her son’s thieving habits better than anyone, but she would rather choke than admit he had brought this doom on himself. Driven mad by shame and grief, she seized a heavy porcelain teacup and hurled it straight at Wei Wuxian's skull. “If you hadn't put on that circus and slandered him in front of the whole town, would he have snuck out in the middle of the night?! It’s all your fault, you dirty bastard!”

Wei Wuxian dodged effortlessly. Thwarted, Madam Mo whipped around to shriek at Lan Sizhui. “And you lot! A pack of useless brats! Call yourselves cultivators? Call yourselves monster hunters?! You couldn't even protect a child! A-Yuan was only a boy!”

The disciples were barely teenagers, out on their very first unsupervised night-hunts. They hadn't detected anything this dangerous lurking in the area, and Mo Ziyuan's death had already weighed on them with guilt. But taking a venomous, unhinged tongue-lashing from a hysterical noblewoman turned their faces an ugly shade of green. Coming from a prestigious lineage, nobody had ever dared speak down to them like this. Yet the Lan clan rules were unforgiving: they were forbidden from raising a hand against helpless mortals, and basic decorum had to be maintained at all costs. Swallowing their temper, they could only stand there, choking on their own fury.

Wei Wuxian, on the other hand, had zero patience for this brand of martyrdom. Typical Lan disciples—all these years later and they’re still choking on their own rigid manners! What good is high-minded discipline if you just stand there taking hits? Watch how it’s done.

He spat loudly onto the flagstones. “Who the hell do you think you’re barking at? You think they’re your household servants? They came all the way out here to clean up your vermin for free, and now they owe you? And how old was your precious boy? Seventeen? Eighteen? That's what you call a child? What kind of seventeen-year-old child can't follow simple human speech?! Didn't they warn everyone repeatedly not to touch the array and stay the hell away from the Western Courtyard? Your son snuck out like a common thief in the dead of night, and that's our fault? That's his fault?!”

Lan Jingyi and the other juniors let out a collective breath, their faces finally regaining some color.

Madam Mo was too far gone in grief and spite to care about logic. Her mind had narrowed down to one single obsession: death. Not hers to join her son, but the deaths of everyone in this room—starting with the people standing before her. Accustomed to bossing her husband around, she shoved him hard. “Call the men! Bring everyone inside, now!”

Her husband, however, remained rooted to the spot, entirely lifeless. Perhaps the shock of losing their only son had shattered his mind, because instead of obeying, he shoved her back. Caught completely off guard, Madam Mo tumbled to the floor in a heap, gaping in stunned disbelief.

Under normal circumstances, the man jumped the second she raised her voice; today, he had actually struck her back.

The servants shrank back, petrified by her expression. A-Ding rushed forward, trembling as she helped her mistress up. Clutching her chest, Madam Mo gasped through rattling breaths, “You… you… get out! Get out of my sight, both of you!”

Her husband gave no sign he’d heard her. A-Ding shot frantic looks at A-Tong, who hurriedly stepped forward, hooking an arm under his master to steer him outside. The hall was descending into utter chaos. Seeing the family feud clear the floor, Wei Wuxian turned back to examine the corpse. He barely got two seconds of quiet before a bloodcurdling scream tore through the outer courtyard.

The entire hall surged through the doors.

Out on the pavers of the Eastern Courtyard, two figures were thrashing on the ground. One was A-Tong, hyperventilating in absolute terror. The other was the husband. His flesh was already withered and sunken, his body shriveled into a dry husk. His left arm was torn clean from the socket, the wound completely bloodless.

He looked identical to Mo Ziyuan.

Madam Mo broke away from A-Ding’s grip, took one look at the withered shell of her husband, and her eyes rolled straight back. Her fury finally ran dry, and she crumpled into a dead faint. Wei Wuxian, who happened to be standing closest, caught her by the shoulder and dumped her into the arms of the scrambling maid. He glanced down at his right wrist.

The second cut had vanished.

The man had barely crossed the threshold before being butchered on the pavers—it had happened in the blink of an eye. Even Lan Sizhui and Lan Jingyi had turned ghost-pale.

Sizhui was the first to regain his footing, rushing over to shake the weeping A-Tong. “Did you see it?! What attacked him?!”

A-Tong was paralyzed with shock, his teeth clattering together so hard he couldn't form a syllable. He could only shake his head frantically. Knowing time was slipping through their fingers, Sizhui signaled his martial brothers to drag the boy inside, then whipped around to Jingyi. “Did you launch the flare?”

“I did!” Lan Jingyi shouted. “But unless a senior cultivator happens to be hunting nearby, our reinforcements won’t get here for at least an hour! What do we do? We don’t even know what the hell we're fighting!”

Running was out of the question. If disciples of a major clan abandoned civilians to save their own skins, they’d not only bring disgrace to their sect, they’d never be able to look themselves in the mirror again. But they couldn't evacuate the terrified villagers either; the entity was likely hiding among them right now.

Lan Sizhui gritted his teeth, his grip tightening on his sword hilt. “Hold the perimeter! We wait for backup!”

With the emergency flare lighting up the sky, allied cultivators would converge on Mo Village before long. By all rights, Wei Wuxian should slip away immediately. If the arriving seniors were strangers, fine, but if someone showed up who knew his face—or worse, who had fought him back in the day—things would turn ugly fast.

Yet with the sacrificial curse binding his soul, he couldn't step foot outside Mo Village. More importantly, whatever had been summoned had claimed two lives in minutes with chilling brutality. If he walked away right now, the reinforcements would arrive only to find a village paved with one-armed corpses—including the Lan clan's precious direct heirs.

Weighing his options, Wei Wuxian let out a grim sigh: Wrap this up, and wrap it up fast.
